3:17 AM.
I know because I'm staring at the clock. Again.
My heart is hammering so hard I can feel it in my throat. The sheets are soaked through. My head is pounding with that familiar, sickening throb that starts behind my eyes and radiates down my neck.
And that taste. God, that taste in my mouth. Like something died in there.
========
But the worst part? The absolute worst part isn't physical.
It's the thoughts.
The spiraling, suffocating thoughts that come flooding in at 3AM when there's nothing to distract you from what you've become.
*Did I say something embarrassing at dinner?*
*Why did my husband give me that look?*
*Did I forget to pick up my daughter from soccer practice? No, wait... that was yesterday.*
*Or was it today?*
========
I reach for my phone. Thirteen unread messages. My stomach drops.
I'm too scared to open them. What if I sent something? What if I called someone? What if I don't remember?
========
This is my life now.
This is what I've become.
And the worst part? Tomorrow, I'll do it all over again.
========
**THE MORNING AFTER (EVERY MORNING AFTER)**
The alarm goes off at 6:30 AM.
I've had maybe two hours of actual sleep. The rest was just... sweaty, anxious half-consciousness punctuated by nightmares I can't quite remember.
I sit up slowly. The room spins.
My hands are shaking so badly I can barely turn off the alarm. I try three times before I manage to swipe correctly.
========
The bathroom mirror is not my friend anymore.
The face staring back at me is puffy. Bloated. My eyes are bloodshot, with dark circles so deep they look like bruises. My skin has this gray, lifeless quality that no amount of makeup can hide.
I'm 38 years old.
I look 52.
========
I grip the sink with both hands and try to breathe. Just breathe.
But my chest is tight. That familiar band of anxiety is already constricting around my ribs, making every breath feel incomplete.
*I can't do this again.*
*I can't keep living like this.*
But I will. Because I always do.

I've been a surgical nurse for 27 years, and male bladder leakage is one of those things nobody talks about in healthcare. Not in the break room. Not at staff meetings. Not even with your closest colleagues.

But I see it every single day.

I see it in the men who come in for follow-up appointments after prostate surgery. The ones who sit down carefully. The ones who shift in their chairs. The ones who glance toward the bathroom the moment they walk through the door.

I see it in the way they hold themselves. Stiff. Controlled. Like they're bracing against something nobody else can see.

I've been assisting in prostatectomies for over two decades. I've watched hundreds of men go into surgery confident and hopeful. Cancer's coming out. Life's going to go back to normal.

And then I see them at their six-week follow-up. Their three-month check. Their one-year review.

Still in pads. Still leaking. Still wearing dark trousers. Still making excuses about why they can't stay long.

The surgeon tells them to keep doing their Kegels. Give it more time. Recovery timelines vary.

I've heard that line so many times I could say it in my sleep.

And every time, I watch the man's face. That flicker of something between frustration and resignation. He nods. He says thank you. He walks out. And I know — I know from 27 years of watching — that most of them are going home to another month of pads and silence.

It's the silence that gets me.

Women talk about incontinence. Not easily, not happily, but they talk. They tell their friends. They tell their doctors. They ask questions.

I've been a parasitologist and I've been administering ivermectin for 13 years, but last month I refused to take one myself.

I want to explain why.

Because there's a sentence I've been unable to say in my professional capacity for over a decade.

And until three months ago, I kept my mouth shut.

I'm not keeping it shut anymore.

My name is Katelyn.

I work in a university parasitology lab attached to a hospital I'm not going to name.

13 years studying the organisms that live inside the human body.

I've examined more infected tissue samples than I can count.

Most of those patients were on ivermectin or some form of antiparasitic prescription.

Most of them had "cleared" status in their chart.

That's the part that broke me eventually.

I just didn't know it yet.

Here's what my job looks like.

A patient gets referred to our lab with unexplained chronic symptoms.

I pull up their chart.

Stool test: negative.

Ova and parasite screen: negative.

They've been on ivermectin or albendazole for one round, maybe two.

Their chart says "treated and cleared."

And they're sitting in front of me still bloated, still exhausted, still waking up at 3am, still foggy, still gaining weight for no reason.

The first few times it happens you tell yourself the parasites are actually gone.

Or the symptoms are psychosomatic.

Or the patient just has IBS like the gastroenterologist wrote.

By year five you stop telling yourself stories.

By year ten you start counting.

I started counting in 2018.

I keep a number in my head now.

I'm not going to share it because it would sound like I'm making it up.

Just trust me when I say it's a lot of people.

A lot of mothers.

A lot of fathers.

A lot of men and women in their thirties, forties, fifties, all who thought they were doing everything right.

All of them "cleared" on paper.

All of them still suffering.

All of them still infected.

And I never said anything.

I want to be honest about that.

"How long has your recession been this severe?" he asks.

My husband asked me to meet him in the church parking lot after second service last Sunday.

Nothing unusual. We've been doing this for years. He finishes up his deacon duties, I finish up with the women's ministry meeting, and we head to dinner.

"Brother James… who is that?"

"When did she… what did she do?"

"Man, the Lord blessed you twice."

"What was that about?" I asked.

After my pedicure, my nail tech asked: 'Can I ask why you do it that way?' I had no idea what she meant. I'm 69 years old.

I've been getting monthly pedicures at the same salon for twelve years.

And I've been apologizing for my legs every single time.

Last Wednesday at 2:15 PM, sitting in the pedicure chair with my feet in warm water, I did it 
again.

"Sorry about the stubble," I said to Tina, my nail tech. "I shaved yesterday but you can 
probably already see it coming back."

I always say this. Every month. For twelve years.

Tina has seen my legs more than anyone except me. The razor burn on my ankles. The 
nicks that take forever to heal. The stubble that's visible by day two no matter how carefully I 
shave.

She's always been polite. Never commented. Just smiled and said "You're fine" and started 
the pedicure.

But this time, she put down the foot file and looked at me.

"Can I tell you something?"

"Sure."

"You're my only client who still shaves their legs."

I stared at her. "What?"

"Out of everyone I see. And I see maybe forty women a week. You're the only one who 
shaves."

I felt my face get hot. "That can't be right."

"It is. You're the only one who apologizes for stubble. The only one with razor burn. The only 
one with nicks healing on their ankles. Everyone else uses cream."

I sat there with my feet in the water feeling like the floor had dropped out.

"Everyone?"

"Every other woman I see. Young, old, doesn't matter. They all use depilatory cream. I 
thought you knew. I've been doing nails for fifteen years. You're the only person who still 
shaves."

I gave my cat taurine every single day for two years to protect her kidneys. Last month her vet told me she's in stage 3 kidney failure. 

More than half her kidney function is already gone.

Years of taurine every morning. Mixed into her food. And her kidneys were quietly failing the entire time I thought I was protecting them.

My name is Debra. I live in Columbus with my husband and our cat Nala. 

She's an 11 year old tabby who has slept on my pillow every single night since I adopted her at 2. 

She follows me into the bathroom. She sits on my laptop when I'm working. 

She is the most annoying, needy, perfect cat I've ever had and I would do anything for her.

About two years ago I started seeing stuff online about kidney problems being the number one killer of cats. 

The stat that got me was "1 in 3 cats will develop it." I looked at Nala and thought ok, not you. I'm going to get ahead of this.

I did what most of you have probably done.

I bought a stainless steel water fountain. Watched her drink from it. Felt good.

Switched her to expensive kibble and wet food. High quality.

And then I found taurine. Saw the research about how cats can't make it on their own. How it's critical for kidney function. Heart function. Everything.

I ordered it. Started giving her 500mg every single morning mixed right into her wet food. She ate it no problem.

Fountain. Wet food. Taurine. Annual vet visits.

data.caption: sringe.com
data.copy:
My mother spent the June heat wave "walking laps at the Walmart for the air conditioning." That's what she told everybody, and everybody thought it was cute. It took me until the second heat wave to figure out what she was actually doing there.

She wasn't there for the air conditioning. She was there for the shopping carts.

My name is Karen. I'm 43. My mother, Dot, is 72, and she lives alone in the house I grew up in outside Springfield, Missouri. If you met her you'd love her — she's the kind of woman who irons her gardening clothes. And she is, I have learned this summer, an absolutely world-class liar about her own health.

Let me walk you through it the way I found it, because the finding is the story.

When the first big heat wave rolled through in May, Mom started her "Walmart walks." Every morning, an hour, sometimes more. She'd announce it like a hobby: "I get my steps in and my air conditioning for free." My brother thought it was adorable. Her doctor, she claimed, thought it was great exercise. I thought nothing of it at all.

Then June came, and that heat dome sat down on the whole middle of the country — the one the news kept saying covered 230 million people — and things stopped adding up.

She skipped the strawberry festival she has attended for thirty consecutive years. Too hot, she said. Fair enough; it was scorching.

She skipped my daughter's outdoor swim meet. Too hot. Okay.

She skipped church twice — church, which is air conditioned — because the parking lot walk was "too much in this heat."

But the Walmart walks? Never missed one. Rain, shine, heat advisory. And one Saturday in late June I finally went with her, and inside of five minutes I understood everything.

My mother walked straight to the carts, took one, and leaned on it. And for the next hour, she moved through that store like a woman on a walker — because that's what the cart was. A walker with plausible deniability. Every so often she'd stop in an aisle, park the cart…

data.caption: tryvisionpure.com
data.copy:
I've assisted in cataract surgeries for over a decade. Which means I’ve seen the "success" rate they never tell you about.

And there's something I believe every cataract patient deserves to hear before going under the knife.

My name is Dr. Jennifer Davis. I’ve spent ten years as a surgical assistant at the Denver Eye Institute.

Let me tell you what "success" ACTUALLY means in a cataract surgery context.

Success means the cataract was removed. Nothing more. Nothing less.

It doesn’t mean what happened next.

10% of patients develop permanent floaters after surgery. Black specks drifting across every bright surface they’ll ever look at.

No fix. No second procedure. Just their new permanent vision.

20% develop a permanently droopy eyelid.

Something they discover the first morning they look in the mirror after recovery. Something nobody mentioned once before they signed the consent form.

And then the one I cannot stop thinking about.

42% of cataract surgery patients develop chronic dry eye afterward.

42.

Not a rare complication. Nearly one in two patients.

Because the incision cuts the corneal nerves responsible for tear production.

And in nearly half of all patients, those nerves never regenerate.

Eyes that burn from the moment they wake up. Drops every single hour just to function. Air conditioning that feels like sandpaper.

For the REST OF THEIR LIVES.

And every time one of those patients came back asking why no one had warned them, I had no answer.

That guilt eats me alive every single time.

Then one patient changed everything.

Her name was Margaret.

She was scheduled for surgery the following Tuesday. I passed her in the hallway during her pre-op appointment and she stopped me.

"Is there anything else I can try?" she asked. "Anything at all before I go through with this?"

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
